Tradeoffs Between Rate and Conditional Content with Encoder-Observed Context

Andrew H. Bond · San Jose State University

HTML rendering of the submission manuscript. The PDF is canonical.

Abstract

An encoder observes a jointly Gaussian pair (Y,V)(Y,V) and describes YY at rate RR for a decoder that sees the description alone; the correlated variable VV is the context. A third party holds a noisy copy S=V+US=V+U of the context, and neither the decoder nor the third party decodes with SS. SS enters through the conditional content L=I(X;X̂∣S)L=I(X;\hat{X}\mid S) of the description: the minimal ideal work, in units of kBTln⁡2k_BT\ln 2, to erase the stored description by a reset mechanism retaining SS. This is Steinberg’s common-reconstruction functional applied to the augmented source X=(Y,V)X=(Y,V) with distortion on YY alone. We evaluate it in closed form: L(D)=12log⁡2g⋆L(D)=\tfrac12\log_2 g^\star, with g⋆g^\star the larger root of an explicit quadratic whose coefficients are set by (D,ρ2,τ2)(D,\rho^2,\tau^2), when YY and VV are scalar linear functionals of an arbitrary-dimensional jointly Gaussian source. The closed form recovers the classical rate–distortion function at ρ=0\rho=0 and Gray’s conditional function as τ2→0\tau^2\to0, and meets Steinberg’s scalar Gaussian formula at the ρ2→1\rho^2\to1 boundary. The function is not determined by the reduced (Y,S)(Y,S) marginal: two instances whose (Y,S)(Y,S) laws are equivalent up to bijective scaling have different LL, so the augmentation is load-bearing. We characterize the exact rate–content region; its Pareto frontier is a two-water-level system. Within the strictly noisy model τ2>0\tau^2>0 the frontier is nondegenerate exactly when 0<ρ2<10<\rho^2<1, and the tradeoff persists at the clean-context boundary. We settle exactly when the natural determinant lower bound is attained. For the doubly symmetric binary source with a binary symmetric context channel the function closes completely through a tilt equation anchored at Gray’s function and the marginal rate–distortion function.

Index Terms: Rate–distortion theory, side information, common reconstruction, conditional mutual information, Landauer principle, Gaussian sources.

I. Introduction

A stored description of data has two prices. The first is its rate, the space the description occupies, and rate–distortion theory prices it against the fidelity the decoder requires. The second is paid at the end of the description’s life: erasing a stored description irreversibly costs work, and when the mechanism performing the reset retains correlated information, the work is governed not by the description’s entropy but by its conditional entropy given what the mechanism holds. The two prices are set by different parties. The decoder never sees the reset mechanism’s information, and the reset mechanism never serves the decoder. This paper solves the source coding problem that this asymmetry creates, for Gaussian and binary sources, in closed form.

The setting is as follows. An encoder observes a jointly Gaussian pair (Y,V)(Y,V): YY is the variable the decoder must reproduce, and VV is a correlated variable, which we call the context (ρ=𝔼[YV]\rho=\mathbb{E}[YV] after normalization). The encoder emits a description under a distortion constraint 𝔼(Y−Ŷ)2≤D\mathbb{E}(Y-\hat{Y})^2\le D that binds the unconditional error; the decoder reconstructs from the description alone. A third party holds S=V+US=V+U, a noisy observation of the context with noise variance τ2\tau^2. The quantity of interest is L(D)=min⁡I(X;X̂∣S)L(D)=\min I(X;\hat{X}\mid S) over test channels satisfying the distortion constraint and the Markov chain X̂−X−S\hat{X}-X-S. We call L(D)L(D) the minimal conditional content of an admissible description; by the operational theorem of Section II it is the least asymptotically achievable value of the normalized conditional entropy H(M∣Sn)/nH(M\mid S^n)/n of the stored index MM among codes meeting the distortion constraint, and hence the minimal ideal erasure work per symbol in units of kBTln⁡2k_BT\ln 2.

The single-letter functional itself is not new. With the augmented source X=(Y,V)X=(Y,V) and a distortion that ignores the VV coordinate, min⁡I(X;X̂∣S)\min I(X;\hat{X}\mid S) is exactly Steinberg’s common-reconstruction functional [12], and Remark 8 of Lapidoth, Malär, and Wigger [13] notes precisely this augmentation device: an encoder observing an additional sequence correlated with the side information is handled by enlarging the source alphabet and letting the distortion ignore the extra coordinate. What this paper adds is, first, an operational reading: L(D)L(D) is the minimal ideal conditional-erasure work of the stored description against a third party that retains SS and never decodes. Second, an evaluation: we solve the augmented Gaussian problem in closed form when YY and VV are scalar linear functionals of an arbitrary-dimensional jointly Gaussian source, where the known Gaussian solutions [12], [13] are scalar and unaugmented. Three classical objects sit at the corners of the closed form. When the described variable and the context decouple (ρ=0\rho=0), LL is Shannon’s rate–distortion function [1]. When the third party’s copy is clean (τ2→0\tau^2\to 0), LL is Gray’s conditional rate–distortion function [4]. When the described variable and the context merge (ρ2→1\rho^2\to 1), LL meets Steinberg’s scalar Gaussian formula at the induced correlation. The augmentation is load-bearing, not cosmetic: we exhibit two instances whose (Y,S)(Y,S) laws are equivalent up to bijective scaling and whose values of LL differ (Section V), so LL is not determined by the reduced marginal (Y,S)(Y,S); the encoder’s access to the clean context VV, which neither the decoder nor the third party shares, enters the function itself.

The results fall into four roles: core results, structural consequences, extensions, and consistency anchors, and the bracketed words in the theorem titles carry the roles. The core results are three. Section IV gives the closed form L(D)=12log⁡2g⋆L(D)=\tfrac12\log_2 g^\star with g⋆g^\star the larger root of an explicit quadratic, together with the achieving channel, after Section III reduces the problem, for YY and VV scalar linear functionals of an arbitrary-dimensional jointly Gaussian source, to the pair (ρ,τ2)(\rho,\tau^2). Section V characterizes the exact region of achievable rate–content pairs, whose Pareto frontier is traced by a two-water-level stationarity system. Section VIII closes the binary case completely: for a doubly symmetric binary source with a binary symmetric context channel, an elementary and self-contained proof yields the function through a tilt equation, anchored at Gray’s binary conditional function at one end and the marginal rate–distortion function at the other. Three structural consequences follow. Within the strictly noisy model τ2>0\tau^2>0 the frontier is nondegenerate, so that rate and content genuinely trade off, exactly when 0<ρ2<10<\rho^2<1, and the tradeoff persists at the clean-context boundary τ2=0\tau^2=0 (Section V). Section VI settles when the natural determinant lower bound is attained, correcting a plausible conjecture: the attainment condition involves the encoder-accessible conditional covariance, not the third party’s. And LL is not determined by the reduced marginal (Y,S)(Y,S) (Section V). Two extensions follow: the frontier at vector context (Section VII) and the operational region theorem proved directly for the Gaussian source (Appendix B). The remaining results are consistency anchors: the three classical corners, the strict suboptimality of marginalization, and an exact information-bottleneck identity for the weighted objective.

Relation to prior formulations

Table I places each main result against its nearest published neighbor. The single-letter functional is inherited: it is Steinberg’s common-reconstruction functional [12], applied unchanged to the augmented source. The augmentation device is also inherited, as Remark 8 of [13]; what is contributed is the evaluation of the reduced problem, and the closed form, the two coupled water levels, the misalignment dichotomy, and the non-determination phenomenon of Corollary 18 are properties of the solution rather than of the reduction. The physical reading leaves the mathematics unchanged: the coordinate H(M∣Sn)/nH(M\mid S^n)/n is characterized by a proved coding theorem (Section II and Appendix B), and the thermodynamic sentence is one consequence of that theorem. The machinery is classical; to our knowledge, no water-filling in this literature carries two coupled levels tied by a common distortion constraint, and the quadratic of Section IV does not appear in it.

Related work

Conditional rate–distortion theory is due to Gray [3], [4]. In that problem both terminals observe the conditioning variable, and RY∣S(D)R_{Y\mid S}(D) prices description under shared context. Here no terminal observes SS; Gray’s function appears only as the clean-context limit τ2→0\tau^2\to0 of our function (Section IV). Wyner and Ziv [5] place the side information at the decoder, where it participates in reconstruction. Our decoder holds nothing but the description, and Wyner–Ziv binning enters the operational theorem of Section II only as a proof device, through a decoder that no party in the model operates.

Steinberg [12] introduced the common-reconstruction constraint: the decoder holds side information, but the encoder must be able to reproduce the decoder’s output exactly. The resulting functional is min⁡I(X;X̂∣S)\min I(X;\hat{X}\mid S) under the Markov chain X̂−X−S\hat{X}-X-S, the single-letter object of this paper, and Steinberg solved its scalar Gaussian case. Lapidoth, Malär, and Wigger [13] relaxed exact to approximate reproduction and solved the Gaussian problem with general jointly Gaussian side information; their Remark 8 notes that an encoder observing an additional correlated sequence is incorporated by augmenting the source and letting the distortion ignore the extra coordinate. Our problem is exactly that augmented problem, with X=(Y,V)X=(Y,V) and distortion on YY alone; Table I delineates what is new relative to this line.

Side information held by the encoder alone is classically inert: when it does not enter the distortion measure, it leaves the rate–distortion function unchanged [2]. Kaspi [10] analyzed the configurations in which the encoder is informed of the side information and the decoder may or may not hold it. In our problem the encoder-held context VV matters despite the classical fact, because the priced coordinate I(X;X̂∣S)I(X;\hat{X}\mid S) is conditional on SS: the encoder never sees SS, but VV is correlated with it, and access to VV strictly lowers the price (Section IV). Heegard and Berger [11] serve decoders with and without side information from one description; Ahmadi, Tandon, Simeone, and Poor [14] imposed the common-reconstruction constraint on the Heegard–Berger and cascade problems and computed Gaussian and binary erased-side-information cases. Section VIII delineates our binary solution from their calculations and from Steinberg’s binary example.

The Gaussian multi-terminal literature under individual distortion constraints supplies the exactness anchor of Section VI: Xiao and Luo [15] derived the joint rate–distortion function of a bivariate Gaussian under individual mean-square constraints, Lapidoth and Tinguely [17] re-derived it, and Nayak, Tuncel, Gündüz, and Erkip [18] and Stylianou, Charalambous, and Charalambous [19] extended the line to successive refinement and to tuples of vector sources. These results enter this paper only at one corner of the attainment condition in Section VI.

The thermodynamic reading of LL rests on Landauer’s principle [24] and its conditional sharpenings [26], [27]; Section II states the operational content and its scope. Task-based quantization [20] and semantic and goal-oriented communication [21] also price descriptions by a downstream objective rather than by reconstruction alone; the structural difference here is the party that holds the conditioning variable and the party that pays for it. The relation to the information bottleneck [23] is exact and worth stating. For any channel with Ŷ−(Y,V)−S\widehat{Y}-(Y,V)-S, writing T=(Y,V)T=(Y,V), the weighted objective traced in Section V collapses by the Markov chain: Jα:=αI(T;Ŷ)+(1−α)I(T;Ŷ∣S)=I(T;Ŷ)−(1−α)I(S;Ŷ),(1)\begin{equation*} J_\alpha:=\alpha I(T;\widehat{Y})+(1-\alpha)I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S) =I(T;\widehat{Y})-(1-\alpha)I(S;\widehat{Y}), \qquad\text{(1)} \end{equation*} an information-bottleneck Lagrangian with tradeoff parameter 1−α1-\alpha, augmented by the hard distortion constraint 𝔼(Y−Ŷ)2≤D\mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat{Y})^2\le D. Gaussian IB [22] establishes the optimality of Gaussian linear-noise representations and the eigenmode structure of the unconstrained Lagrangian. The hard YY-distortion constraint changes the program: it binds a reconstruction error, not a mutual information, and the two-water-level frontier with its distortion price is what the constraint adds. Our Gaussian exhaustion lemma (Section IV) plays the role here that the Gaussian-optimality theorem plays there.

Finally, [28] is a preliminary related manuscript by the author, archived at the repository record of the title footnote. The operational region theorem for discrete sources (Section II) and its single-letterization appeared there, as did the scalar Gaussian corner used in Section IV. Everything from Section III onward is new here: pair sufficiency, the closed form, the region and its frontier, the determinant-bound exactness, vector context, the binary solution, and the Gaussian operational theorem of Appendix B. The present paper supersedes the source-coding content of that record, which remains the archived evidence artifact.

II. Problem Formulation and the Operational Theorem

All logarithms are base two. Random variables have finite alphabets unless a Gaussian specialization is stated. The model has one source and three parties, and Fig. 1 shows it. Let (X,S)∼pXS(X,S)\sim p_{XS}, and let (Xn,Sn)(X^n,S^n) be i.i.d. copies. In the Gaussian sections the source letter is the pair X=(Y,V)X=(Y,V), with YY the described variable and VV the context, and the side information is S=V+US=V+U with UU independent of XX; the operational theorem of this section needs no such structure. The encoder observes XnX^n alone and emits the description MM. The decoder observes MM alone and outputs the reproduction; the general discrete theorem below reproduces the full letter, X̂n\widehat{X}^{n}, while in the Gaussian sections the reproduction is a scalar estimate Ŷ\widehat{Y} of YY alone. The reset mechanism, which is the third party of Section I, retains SnS^n, which remains unchanged by the reset, and accesses the stored index MM in order to erase it; it never decodes.

A distortion measure is a bounded function d:𝒳×𝒳̂→[0,dmax].(2)\begin{equation*} d:\mathcal{X}\times\widehat{\mathcal{X}}\longrightarrow[0,d_{\max}]. \qquad\text{(2)} \end{equation*} An (n,ℳn)(n,\mathcal M_n) observation code consists of an encoder and decoder fn:𝒳n→ℳn,gn:ℳn→𝒳̂n.(3)\begin{equation*} f_n:\mathcal{X}^n\to\mathcal M_n, \qquad g_n:\mathcal M_n\to\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{n}. \qquad\text{(3)} \end{equation*} We write M=fn(Xn)M=f_n(X^n) and X̂n=gn(M)\widehat{X}^{n}=g_n(M). Randomized encoders do not improve the region below, but allowing them in the converse is harmless.

The three operational quantities are Rn=1nlog⁡|ℳn|,(4)Dn=1n∑i=1n𝔼d(Xi,X̂i),(5)Ln=1nH(M∣Sn).(6)\begin{align*} R_n&=\frac{1}{n}\log |\mathcal M_n|, \qquad\text{(4)}\\ D_n&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\,d(X_i,\widehat{X}_i), \qquad\text{(5)}\\ L_n&=\frac{1}{n}H(M\mid S^n). \qquad\text{(6)} \end{align*} The dimensionless quantity LnL_n is the Landauer content of the memory relative to the retained side information. Under an ideal conditional reset, the average work satisfies Wn≥nkBTln⁡2Ln.(7)\begin{equation*} W_n\ \ge\ nk_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln2\,L_n. \qquad\text{(7)} \end{equation*} In the classical asymptotic regime, conditional erasure protocols make this bound tight up to sublinear terms [26], [27]. We therefore state the coding theorem in bits per source symbol and restore physical units by multiplying by kBTln⁡2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln2. The bound (7) prices only the logically irreversible reset of the volatile index MM; it does not count the work of acquiring XnX^n, driving a channel, correcting errors, or finishing in finite time [24], [25]. The codebook, wiring, and any permanent lookup tables are treated as part of the apparatus and are not erased in each cycle.

Definition 1 (Achievability). A triple (R,L,D)(R,L,D) is achievable if there is a sequence of observation codes such that limsupn→∞Rn≤R,limsupn→∞Ln≤L,limsupn→∞Dn≤D.(8)\begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}R_n\le R,\qquad \limsup_{n\to\infty}L_n\le L,\qquad \limsup_{n\to\infty}D_n\le D. \qquad\text{(8)} \end{equation*} The closure of the achievable set at distortion DD is denoted ℛ𝒲(D)\mathcal{R}\!\mathcal{W}(D).

For a test channel p(x̂∣x)p(\hat x\mid x), the Markov chain X̂−X−S\widehat{X}-X-S holds because side information is unavailable when the observation is formed. Define 𝒯(D)={p(x̂∣x):𝔼d(X,X̂)≤D}.(9)\begin{equation*} \mathcal T(D) =\left\{p(\hat x\mid x):\mathbb{E}d(X,\widehat{X})\le D\right\}. \qquad\text{(9)} \end{equation*} The two single-letter functions of the paper are the classical rate–distortion function and the work endpoint, Rmin(D)=minp(x̂∣x)∈𝒯(D)I(X;X̂),L(D)=minp(x̂∣x)∈𝒯(D)I(X;X̂∣S).(10)\begin{equation*} R_{\min}(D)=\min_{p(\hat x\mid x)\in\mathcal T(D)}I(X;\widehat{X}), \qquad L(D)=\min_{p(\hat x\mid x)\in\mathcal T(D)}I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S). \qquad\text{(10)} \end{equation*} Both minima exist by compactness of 𝒯(D)\mathcal T(D) and continuity of the two coordinates. The coding theorem below gives both functions their operational meaning. The following box fixes the two notational scopes of the paper.

Definition 2 (The problem in one box). General letters, used for the discrete theorem of this section: source (X,S)∼pXS(X,S)\sim p_{XS}, i.i.d. copies (Xn,Sn)(X^n,S^n), test channel p(x̂∣x)p(\hat x\mid x) with the Markov chain X̂−X−S\widehat{X}-X-S, constraint set 𝒯(D)\mathcal T(D), and the two functions of (10). Gaussian letters, used from Section III on: the source letter is the jointly Gaussian pair T=(Y,V)T=(Y,V) with Var⁡Y=Var⁡V=1\operatorname{Var}Y=\operatorname{Var}V=1 and 𝔼[YV]=ρ\mathbb{E}[YV]=\rho; the context copy is generated as S=V+US=V+U with U∼𝒩(0,τ2)U\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2) independent of everything else; the test channel is PŶ∣TP_{\widehat{Y}\mid T}, the reproduction Ŷ\widehat{Y} does not see SS, and the Markov chain is Ŷ−T−S\widehat{Y}-T-S; the constraint is 𝔼(Y−Ŷ)2≤D\mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat{Y})^2\le D; and Rmin(D)=min⁡I(T;Ŷ),L(D)=min⁡I(T;Ŷ∣S),R_{\min}(D)=\min I(T;\widehat{Y}), \qquad L(D)=\min I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S), both minima over test channels meeting the constraint.

Lemma 3 (Convexity in the test channel). For fixed pXSp_{XS}, both coordinates I(X;X̂)I(X;\widehat{X}) and I(X;X̂∣S)I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S) are convex functions of the test channel q(x̂∣x)q(\hat x\mid x).

Proof. Convexity of I(X;X̂)I(X;\widehat{X}) in the channel at fixed input is classical. For the conditional coordinate, the Markov chain X̂−X−S\widehat{X}-X-S gives p(x̂∣x,s)=q(x̂∣x)p(\hat x\mid x,s)=q(\hat x\mid x), so I(X;X̂∣S)=∑sp(s)Ip(x∣s)(q),(11)\begin{equation*} I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)=\sum_s p(s)\,I_{p(x\mid s)}(q), \qquad\text{(11)} \end{equation*} a nonnegative combination of mutual informations, each with fixed input distribution p(x∣s)p(x\mid s) and the common channel qq; each term is convex in qq, hence so is the sum. We note that the decomposition I(X;X̂∣S)=I(X;X̂)−I(S;X̂)I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)=I(X;\widehat{X})-I(S;\widehat{X}) does not yield this conclusion: I(S;X̂)I(S;\widehat{X}) is itself convex in qq (the induced channel p(x̂∣s)=∑xp(x∣s)q(x̂∣x)p(\hat x\mid s)=\sum_x p(x\mid s)q(\hat x\mid x) is linear in qq), so the difference is a priori indefinite.

□

Theorem 4 (Rate–work–distortion region). For a discrete memoryless source (X,S)(X,S) and bounded distortion dd, ℛ𝒲(D)=⋃p(x̂∣x)∈𝒯(D){(R,L):R≥I(X;X̂),L≥I(X;X̂∣S)}.(12)\begin{equation*} \mathcal{R}\!\mathcal{W}(D) =\bigcup_{p(\hat x\mid x)\in\mathcal T(D)} \left\{(R,L): R\ge I(X;\widehat{X}),\ L\ge I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S) \right\}. \qquad\text{(12)} \end{equation*} The physical reset-work coordinate is W/n=kBTln⁡2LW/n=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln2\,L in the ideal model. By Lemma 3 the union is already convex, and it is closed by compactness of 𝒯(D)\mathcal T(D) and continuity of both coordinates; no time sharing is required, and every boundary point is attained by a single test channel.

Proof. We first prove the converse. Let a code produce MM and X̂n\widehat{X}^{n}. Since X̂n\widehat{X}^{n} is a function of MM, log⁡|ℳn|≥H(M)≥I(Xn;M)≥I(Xn;X̂n)≥∑i=1nI(Xi;X̂i),(13)\begin{align*} \log|\mathcal M_n| &\ge H(M)\ge I(X^n;M)\ge I(X^n;\widehat{X}^{n})\\ &\ge \sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_i;\widehat{X}_i), \qquad\text{(13)} \end{align*} where the last step follows from memorylessness and conditioning reducing entropy (Appendix A). Likewise, H(M∣Sn)≥I(Xn;M∣Sn)≥I(Xn;X̂n∣Sn)≥∑i=1nI(Xi;X̂i∣Si).(14)\begin{align*} H(M\mid S^n) &\ge I(X^n;M\mid S^n) \ge I(X^n;\widehat{X}^{n}\mid S^n)\\ &\ge \sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_i;\widehat{X}_i\mid S_i). \qquad\text{(14)} \end{align*} Each induced per-letter channel p(x̂i∣xi)p(\hat x_i\mid x_i) satisfies the Markov constraint X̂i−Xi−Si\widehat{X}_i-X_i-S_i: X̂i\widehat{X}_i is a function of (Xi,X≠i)(X_i,X_{\ne i}) and SiS_i is independent of X≠iX_{\ne i} given XiX_i for i.i.d. pairs. Let q‾(x̂∣x)=1n∑i=1np(x̂i=x̂∣Xi=x)\bar q(\hat x\mid x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}p(\hat x_i=\hat x\mid X_i=x) be the mixture channel; the constraint survives the mixture because p(s∣x)p(s\mid x) is common across ii. Its distortion is DnD_n, so q‾∈𝒯(Dn)\bar q\in\mathcal T(D_n), and by Lemma 3, Rn≥1n∑iI(Xi;X̂i)≥Iq‾(X;X̂),Ln≥1n∑iI(Xi;X̂i∣Si)≥Iq‾(X;X̂∣S),\begin{equation*} R_n\ \ge\ \frac1n\sum_i I(X_i;\widehat{X}_i)\ \ge\ I_{\bar q}(X;\widehat{X}), \qquad L_n\ \ge\ \frac1n\sum_i I(X_i;\widehat{X}_i\mid S_i)\ \ge\ I_{\bar q}(X;\widehat{X}\mid S), \end{equation*} which places (Rn,Ln)(R_n,L_n) in the (already convex and closed) union of (12) at distortion DnD_n. To pass from DnD_n to DD: for an achievable triple limsup⁡Dn≤D\limsup D_n\le D, the right side of (12) is monotone in the distortion level, and it is right-continuous in it, because 𝒯(D)=⋂D′>D𝒯(D′)\mathcal T(D)=\bigcap_{D'>D}\mathcal T(D') with each 𝒯(D′)\mathcal T(D') compact and both coordinates continuous, so the intersection of the regions over D′>DD'>D is the region at DD; hence every limit point of (Rn,Ln)(R_n,L_n), and with it (R,L)(R,L), lies in the right side of (12) at DD.

For achievability, fix p(x̂∣x)∈𝒯(D)p(\hat x\mid x)\in\mathcal T(D) and ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Generate a random codebook 𝒞\mathcal C of 2n(I(X;X̂)+2ϵ)2^{n(I(X;\widehat{X})+2\epsilon)} independent x̂n\hat x^n codewords drawn from the X̂\widehat{X}-marginal, and, independently, a random binning bb assigning each codeword index uniformly to one of 2n(I(X;X̂∣S)+3ϵ)2^{n(I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)+3\epsilon)} bins. The covering encoder selects a codeword jointly (strongly) typical with xnx^n, declaring failure otherwise, and stores its index MM; the decoder reconstructs the codeword from MM alone. Two failure events. First, EcovE_{\mathrm{cov}}: no jointly typical codeword exists; Pr⁡(Ecov)→0\Pr(E_{\mathrm{cov}})\to0, averaged over (Xn,𝒞)(X^n,\mathcal C), by the covering lemma, and on EcovcE_{\mathrm{cov}}^{\mathrm c} the distortion is at most D+ϵD+\epsilon by typicality. Second, EbinE_{\mathrm{bin}}: the side-information proof device fails. Because X̂−X−S\widehat{X}-X-S, I(X;X̂∣S)=I(X;X̂)−I(S;X̂),(15)\begin{equation*} I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)=I(X;\widehat{X})-I(S;\widehat{X}), \qquad\text{(15)} \end{equation*} so each bin holds 2n(I(S;X̂)−ϵ)2^{n(I(S;\widehat{X})-\epsilon)} codewords on average, a per-bin codeword rate ϵ\epsilon below the packing threshold I(S;X̂)I(S;\widehat{X}), and the Wyner–Ziv packing argument [5] (the Markov lemma for the typicality of the selected codeword with SnS^n, and the packing bound for wrong codewords in the bin) gives a decoder that recovers MM from (B,Sn)(B,S^n), B=b(M)B=b(M), with Pr⁡(Ebin)→0\Pr(E_{\mathrm{bin}})\to0 averaged over (Xn,Sn,𝒞,b)(X^n,S^n,\mathcal C,b). This decoder is a proof device; the actual decoder of the code still receives no side information.

Selection of one deterministic code. Let ϵn:=𝔼𝒞,b[Pr⁡(Ecov∣𝒞)+Pr⁡(Ebin∣𝒞,b)]→0\epsilon_n:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal C,b}\bigl[\Pr(E_{\mathrm{cov}}\mid\mathcal C) +\Pr(E_{\mathrm{bin}}\mid\mathcal C,b)\bigr]\to0. By Markov’s inequality there is a deterministic pair (𝒞,b)(\mathcal C,b) with Pr⁡(Ecov)+Pr⁡(Ebin)≤2ϵn\Pr(E_{\mathrm{cov}})+\Pr(E_{\mathrm{bin}})\le2\epsilon_n. Fix it. Its distortion satisfies Dn≤D+ϵ+2ϵndmaxD_n\le D+\epsilon+2\epsilon_n d_{\max}, and by Fano’s inequality applied to the proof device on this fixed code, H(M∣B,Sn)≤1+2ϵnlog⁡|ℳn|=1+2ϵnn(I(X;X̂)+2ϵ)H(M\mid B,S^n)\le1+2\epsilon_n\log|\mathcal M_n| =1+2\epsilon_n\,n\bigl(I(X;\widehat{X})+2\epsilon\bigr), so H(M∣Sn)≤H(B)+H(M∣B,Sn)≤n(I(X;X̂∣S)+3ϵ)+1+2ϵnn(I(X;X̂)+2ϵ)=n(I(X;X̂∣S)+3ϵ+o(1)).(16)\begin{align*} H(M\mid S^n) &\le H(B)+H(M\mid B,S^n)\\ &\le n\bigl(I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)+3\epsilon\bigr) +1+2\epsilon_n\,n\bigl(I(X;\widehat{X})+2\epsilon\bigr) \;=\;n\bigl(I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)+3\epsilon+o(1)\bigr). \qquad\text{(16)} \end{align*} The selected deterministic code thus satisfies the distortion and the conditional-entropy requirements simultaneously: the stored index has ordinary description rate I(X;X̂)+2ϵI(X;\widehat{X})+2\epsilon, distortion at most D+ϵ+o(1)D+\epsilon+o(1), and conditional Landauer content at most I(X;X̂∣S)+3ϵ+o(1)I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)+3\epsilon+o(1). Letting ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow0 along a diagonal sequence of blocklengths exhibits the corner (I(X;X̂),I(X;X̂∣S))\bigl(I(X;\widehat{X}),I(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)\bigr) at distortion DD; since the union in (12) is already convex and closed (Lemma 3), this exhibits the entire region.

□

The binning step in the proof has a simple interpretation. The full codeword index is required by the decoder. At reset, side information identifies the codeword up to a bin of asymptotic size 2nI(X;X̂∣S)2^{nI(X;\widehat{X}\mid S)}. Only that residual uncertainty is thermodynamically irreducible. The step has also been verified numerically at finite blocklength (Appendix C).

The work-only endpoint of the region is the minimum Landauer content, the function L(D)L(D) defined in (10). As an information quantity, L(D)L(D) is Steinberg’s common-reconstruction rate–distortion function for side information SS [12]: the reproduction must be determined without access to SS. The operational roles differ. In the common-reconstruction problem, SS is decoder side information that must not corrupt reproducibility; here SS is held by a reset mechanism that never serves the decoder. The remainder of the paper characterizes L(D)L(D), and the region around it, for the source of Section III.

Remark 5 (The Gaussian pair specialization). From Section III on, the source letter is the jointly Gaussian pair X=(Y,V)X=(Y,V) introduced there, and the distortion is d(x,x̂)=(y−ŷ)2d(x,\hat x)=(y-\hat y)^2 on the YY coordinate: the decoder is judged on YY alone, while the encoder observes the pair.

Remark 6 (Scope of the coding theorem). Theorem 4 is stated and proved for finite alphabets and bounded per-letter distortion. For the jointly Gaussian source of Section III with quadratic distortion on the described variable, the corresponding operational statement is Theorem 27 in Appendix B: the converse is proved there in full, and the achievability by reduction to quantized side information, with two classical probabilistic ingredients imported under precise citations. The Gaussian closed forms of Sections III–VI are evaluations of the single-letter coordinates in (12), and their operational meaning is inherited through Theorem 27.

III. Pair Sufficiency

Let X∼𝒩(0,Σx)X\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_x) on ℝd\mathbb{R}^d, i.i.d. across source symbols. The described variable is the linear functional Y=w𝖳XY=w^{\mathsf T}X; the third party’s copy is a second linear functional observed in noise, S=γ𝖳X+US=\gamma^{\mathsf T}X+U. Normalize Var⁡(w𝖳X)=1\operatorname{Var}(w^{\mathsf T}X)=1 (rescaling DD), write V=γ𝖳X/σγV=\gamma^{\mathsf T}X/\sigma_{\gamma}, the normalized context, with ρ:=𝔼[YV]\rho:=\mathbb{E}[YV], |ρ|<1|\rho|<1, and rescale SS (invariantly for all mutual informations) to S=V+US=V+U, U∼𝒩(0,τ2)U\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2), τ2>0\tau^2>0. Write s=1+τ2s=1+\tau^2. Throughout, XX, UU, and all channel randomness (including any resampling randomness below) are mutually independent. This joint form of the independence assumption is load-bearing: it is exactly what the SS-kernel argument in the next proof uses.

From here on the Gaussian scope of Definition 2 is in force: the ambient source is XX, the pair is T=(Y,V)T=(Y,V), the reproduction is Ŷ\widehat{Y}, and once Theorem 7 below is proved, all information quantities are written on (T,Ŷ,S)(T,\widehat{Y},S). Reproductions may be taken scalar without loss of optimality: replacing X̂\widehat{X} by Ŷ:=w𝖳X̂\widehat{Y}:=w^{\mathsf T}\widehat{X} leaves the distortion unchanged and can only decrease I(X;⋅∣S)I(X;\cdot\mid S) (conditional data processing), and Ŷ−X−S\widehat{Y}-X-S persists.

Theorem 7 (Pair sufficiency). In the problem L(D)=min⁡{I(X;Ŷ∣S):Ŷ−X−S,𝔼(Y−Ŷ)2≤D}L(D)=\min\{I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S):\widehat{Y}-X-S,\ \mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat{Y})^2\le D\}, it is without loss of optimality to let the channel depend on XX only through T=(Y,V)T=(Y,V), and then I(X;Ŷ∣S)=I(T;Ŷ∣S)I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S)=I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S). Consequently L(D)L(D) depends on (Σx,w,γ,τ2)(\Sigma_x,w,\gamma,\tau^2), for the scalar linear functionals Y=w𝖳XY=w^{\mathsf T}X and V=γ𝖳X/σγV=\gamma^{\mathsf T}X/\sigma_\gamma of a source of arbitrary dimension dd, only through (ρ,τ2)(\rho,\tau^2).

Proof. Given an admissible p(ŷ∣x)p(\hat y\mid x), draw Ŷ′\widehat{Y}' from the conditional law p(ŷ∣T=t)p(\hat y\mid T=t) using fresh randomness. (a) (T,Ŷ′)=d(T,Ŷ)(T,\widehat{Y}')\overset{d}= (T,\widehat{Y}), so the distortion (a functional of (Y,Ŷ)(Y,\widehat{Y})) is unchanged. (b) S=V+US=V+U with UU independent of (X,Ŷ)(X,\widehat{Y}) and of (X,Ŷ′)(X,\widehat{Y}'), so in both joints p(s∣t,ŷ)=pU(s−v)p(s\mid t,\hat y)=p_U(s-v): hence (T,Ŷ′,S)=d(T,Ŷ,S)(T,\widehat{Y}',S)\overset{d}=(T,\widehat{Y},S). (c) Given TT, Ŷ′\widehat{Y}' is independent of (X,S)(X,S), so I(X;Ŷ′∣S)=I(T;Ŷ′∣S)+I(X;Ŷ′∣T,S)=I(T;Ŷ∣S)≤I(X;Ŷ∣S)I(X;\widehat{Y}'\mid S)=I(T;\widehat{Y}'\mid S)+I(X;\widehat{Y}'\mid T,S) =I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S)\le I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S), the last step because TT is a function of XX. (d) Ŷ′−X−S\widehat{Y}'-X-S holds since Ŷ′\widehat{Y}' is a function of (X,fresh noise)(X,\text{fresh noise}) with the noise independent of (X,U)(X,U). The same computation applied to a TT-channel directly gives I(X;Ŷ∣S)=I(T;Ŷ∣S)I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S)=I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S).

□

IV. The Function: Scalar Context

One further reduction identifies the class the closed form must beat. (Marginalized class == scalar corner.) If the channel depends on XX only through YY (that is, Ŷ−Y−(X,S)\widehat{Y}-Y-(X,S)), then given (Y,S)(Y,S), Ŷ\widehat{Y} is independent of XX, so I(X;Ŷ∣S)=I(Y;Ŷ∣S)I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S)=I(Y;\widehat{Y}\mid S), and the class optimum is exactly the scalar-corner value 12log⁡2[(σ2(1−ρYS2)+ρYS2D)/D]\tfrac12\log_2\bigl[(\sigma^2(1-\rho_{YS}^2)+\rho_{YS}^2D)/D\bigr] of the pair (Y,S)(Y,S), where σ2=Var⁡Y\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}Y and ρYS\rho_{YS} is the correlation of that pair, ρYS2=ρ2/s\rho_{YS}^2=\rho^2/s after the normalization of Section III [12]; the corner’s converse applies to every p(ŷ∣y)p(\hat y\mid y), discrete or not.

Proposition 8 (Anchor: marginalization is strictly suboptimal). Let d=2d=2, X∼𝒩(0,I2)X\sim\mathcal N(0,I_2), Y=X1Y=X_1, and S=X1+X2S=X_1+X_2 (so ρYS2=12\rho^2_{YS}=\tfrac12 and SS is XX-measurable). For 0<D<10<D<1:

  1. the marginalized-class optimum is the scalar corner Lmarg(D)=12log⁡21+D2DL_{\mathrm{marg}}(D)=\tfrac12\log_2\!\frac{1+D}{2D};

  2. the vector problem has the exact value Lvec(D)=12log⁡2+12D=RY∣S(D),L_{\mathrm{vec}}(D)\;=\;\tfrac12\log_2^{+}\!\frac{1}{2D} \;=\;R_{Y\mid S}(D), Gray’s conditional rate–distortion function of (Y,S)(Y,S) [4] (Var⁡(Y∣S)=12\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid S)=\tfrac12), attained by the linear channel Ŷ=(1−D)X1+DX2+N\widehat{Y}=(1-D)X_1+DX_2+N, N∼𝒩(0,D(1−2D))N\sim\mathcal N(0,D(1-2D)), for D≤12D\le\tfrac12, and by Ŷ=S/2\widehat{Y}=S/2 (zero conditional content) for D≥12D\ge\tfrac12;

  3. hence the strict gap Lmarg(D)−Lvec(D)=12log⁡2(1+D)>0L_{\mathrm{marg}}(D)-L_{\mathrm{vec}}(D)=\tfrac12\log_2(1+D)>0 on (0,12](0,\tfrac12], and equal to the full marginalized value on [12,1)[\tfrac12,1) (where Lvec=0L_{\mathrm{vec}}=0; the absolute gap is decreasing there, but it is all of LmargL_{\mathrm{marg}}).

Proof. (i) is the reduction above, evaluated at σ2=1\sigma^2=1, ρYS2=12\rho_{YS}^2=\tfrac12.

(ii) Converse. For any admissible Ŷ\widehat{Y} (Markov Ŷ−X−S\widehat{Y}-X-S), I(X;Ŷ∣S)≥I(Y;Ŷ∣S)I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S)\ge I(Y;\widehat{Y}\mid S), and the induced conditional channel p(ŷ∣y,s)p(\hat y\mid y,s) is feasible for Gray’s conditional problem at the same distortion, so I(Y;Ŷ∣S)≥RY∣S(D)=12log⁡2+(Var⁡(Y∣S)/D)=12log⁡2+(1/(2D))I(Y;\widehat{Y}\mid S)\ge R_{Y\mid S}(D)=\tfrac12\log_2^{+} \bigl(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid S)/D\bigr)=\tfrac12\log_2^{+}(1/(2D)). Achievability. For D≤12D\le\tfrac12 take Ŷ=(1−D)X1+DX2+N\widehat{Y}=(1-D)X_1+DX_2+N: distortion D2+D2+D(1−2D)=DD^2+D^2+D(1-2D)=D; Var⁡(Ŷ)=1−D\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{Y})=1-D, Cov⁡(Ŷ,S)=1\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{Y},S)=1, Var⁡(Ŷ∣S)=1−D−12=12−D\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{Y}\mid S)=1-D-\tfrac12=\tfrac12-D, so I(X;Ŷ∣S)=12log⁡2(1−2D)/2D(1−2D)=12log⁡212DI(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S)=\tfrac12\log_2\frac{(1-2D)/2}{D(1-2D)} =\tfrac12\log_2\frac1{2D}. For D≥12D\ge\tfrac12, Ŷ=S/2\widehat{Y}=S/2 is a deterministic function of XX, has distortion 𝔼((X1−X2)/2)2=12≤D\mathbb{E}\bigl((X_1-X_2)/2\bigr)^2=\tfrac12\le D, and is constant given SS, so I(X;Ŷ∣S)=0I(X;\widehat{Y}\mid S)=0.

(iii) Subtract. The closed forms on both sides have been verified numerically.

□

The closed form occupies the rest of this section. By Theorem 7 we restrict to TT-channels, T=(Y,V)T=(Y,V), with scalar reproduction Ŷ\widehat{Y}. The working coordinates deserve a plain statement before the machinery. Every jointly Gaussian test channel takes the form Ŷ=aY+bV+N\widehat{Y}=aY+bV+N with NN independent noise of variance nn, and every admissible channel, Gaussian or not, is measured through the same three moments of its regression on TT: the unconditional signal part Q0=Var⁡(aY+bV)Q_0=\operatorname{Var}(aY+bV), the SS-conditional signal part Q1=Var⁡(aY+bV∣S)Q_1=\operatorname{Var}(aY+bV\mid S), and the noise-free distortion contribution h=Var⁡((1−a)Y−bV)h=\operatorname{Var}\bigl((1-a)Y-bV\bigr), so that 𝔼(Y−Ŷ)2=h+n\mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat{Y})^2=h+n. Everything from here through Section VII is expressed in (a,b,n)(a,b,n) and these moments; Table II collects them. The converse rests on one estimation-theoretic lemma. We state it for vector reproductions and vector conditioners, in the generality that Sections V, VI, and VII reuse.

Lemma 9 (Gaussian exhaustion and the determinant identity).

Let (T,S)(T,S) be jointly Gaussian and centered, T∈ℝpT\in\mathbb{R}^p, S∈ℝrS\in\mathbb{R}^r, with Cov⁡((T,S))≻0\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((T,S)\bigr)\succ0. Let 𝐘̂∈ℝm\hat{\mathbf Y}\in\mathbb{R}^m be any centered random vector with finite second moments, and define A:=Cov⁡(𝐘̂,T)ΣT−1∈ℝm×p,N′:=𝐘̂−AT,ΣN:=Cov⁡(N′)=Cov⁡(𝐘̂)−AΣTA𝖳.A:=\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y},T)\,\Sigma_T^{-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p},\qquad N':=\hat{\mathbf Y}-AT,\qquad \Sigma_N:=\operatorname{Cov}(N')=\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y})-A\Sigma_TA^{\mathsf T}. Assume ΣN≻0\Sigma_N\succ0 and Cov⁡(N′,S)=0\operatorname{Cov}(N',S)=0. Then I(T;𝐘̂∣S)≥12log⁡2det⁡ΣT∣Sdet⁡Σe=12log⁡2det⁡(AΣT∣SA𝖳+ΣN)det⁡ΣN,(17)\begin{equation*} I(T;\hat{\mathbf Y}\mid S)\;\ge\;\tfrac12\log_2 \frac{\det\Sigma_{T\mid S}}{\det\Sigma_e} \;=\;\tfrac12\log_2 \frac{\det\bigl(A\Sigma_{T\mid S}A^{\mathsf T}+\Sigma_N\bigr)} {\det\Sigma_N}, \qquad\text{(17)} \end{equation*} where ΣT∣S=ΣT−ΣTSΣS−1ΣST\Sigma_{T\mid S}=\Sigma_T-\Sigma_{TS}\Sigma_S^{-1}\Sigma_{ST} and Σe\Sigma_e is the error covariance of the best linear estimator of TT from (𝐘̂,S)(\hat{\mathbf Y},S). With SS deleted throughout, the hypothesis Cov⁡(N′,S)=0\operatorname{Cov}(N',S)=0 becomes vacuous and the same argument gives I(T;𝐘̂)≥12log⁡2det⁡(AΣTA𝖳+ΣN)det⁡ΣN.(18)\begin{equation*} I(T;\hat{\mathbf Y})\;\ge\;\tfrac12\log_2 \frac{\det\bigl(A\Sigma_TA^{\mathsf T}+\Sigma_N\bigr)}{\det\Sigma_N}. \qquad\text{(18)} \end{equation*} The jointly Gaussian channel 𝐘̂=AT+N\hat{\mathbf Y}=AT+N, N∼𝒩(0,ΣN)N\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_N) independent of (T,S)(T,S), realizes the same second moments and attains both bounds with equality simultaneously.

Proof. Step 1: the max-entropy bound. Write M:=Cov⁡((𝐘̂,S))M:=\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((\hat{\mathbf Y},S)\bigr) and J:=Cov⁡(T,(𝐘̂,S))∈ℝp×(m+r)J:=\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(T,(\hat{\mathbf Y},S)\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times(m+r)}. First, M≻0M\succ0: by the Schur-complement criterion on M=[Cov⁡(𝐘̂)Cov⁡(𝐘̂,S)Cov⁡(S,𝐘̂)ΣS],M=\begin{bmatrix} \operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y})&\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y},S)\\[2pt] \operatorname{Cov}(S,\hat{\mathbf Y})&\Sigma_S \end{bmatrix}, positivity is equivalent to ΣS≻0\Sigma_S\succ0 together with Cov⁡(𝐘̂)−Cov⁡(𝐘̂,S)ΣS−1Cov⁡(S,𝐘̂)≻0\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y})-\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y},S)\Sigma_S^{-1} \operatorname{Cov}(S,\hat{\mathbf Y})\succ0; the first holds because Cov⁡((T,S))≻0\operatorname{Cov}((T,S))\succ0, and the second is evaluated in Step 2 to equal AΣT∣SA𝖳+ΣN≽ΣN≻0A\Sigma_{T\mid S}A^{\mathsf T}+\Sigma_N\succeq\Sigma_N\succ0. The best linear estimator of TT from (𝐘̂,S)(\hat{\mathbf Y},S) is T̂=JM−1(𝐘̂;S)\widehat T=JM^{-1}(\hat{\mathbf Y};S), with error covariance Σe=ΣT−JM−1J𝖳\Sigma_e=\Sigma_T-JM^{-1}J^{\mathsf T}. Since (T,S)(T,S) is jointly Gaussian, h(T∣S)=12log⁡2((2πe)pdet⁡ΣT∣S)h(T\mid S)=\tfrac12\log_2\bigl((2\pi e)^p\det\Sigma_{T\mid S}\bigr) exactly. For the other term, translation invariance of differential entropy, conditioning reduces entropy, and the Gaussian maximum-entropy bound at fixed covariance give h(T∣𝐘̂,S)=h(T−T̂|𝐘̂,S)≤h(T−T̂)≤12log⁡2((2πe)pdet⁡Σe)h(T\mid\hat{\mathbf Y},S) =h\bigl(T-\widehat T\;\big|\;\hat{\mathbf Y},S\bigr) \;\le\;h\bigl(T-\widehat T\bigr) \;\le\;\tfrac12\log_2\bigl((2\pi e)^p\det\Sigma_e\bigr) (with the usual convention that h=−∞h=-\infty for laws without a density, in which case the bound is trivial). Subtracting the two displays inside I(T;𝐘̂∣S)=h(T∣S)−h(T∣𝐘̂,S)I(T;\hat{\mathbf Y}\mid S)=h(T\mid S)-h(T\mid\hat{\mathbf Y},S) yields the inequality in (17).

Step 2: the determinant identity. Let K:=Cov⁡((T,S,𝐘̂))K:=\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((T,S,\hat{\mathbf Y})\bigr). The residual N′N' is uncorrelated with TT by construction of the regression and with SS by hypothesis, and the change of variables (T,S,𝐘̂)↦(T,S,N′)(T,S,\hat{\mathbf Y})\mapsto(T,S,N') is block lower triangular with unit diagonal, hence determinant preserving: det⁡K=det⁡Cov⁡((T,S,N′))=det⁡[ΣTΣTS0ΣSTΣS000ΣN]=det⁡ΣSdet⁡ΣT∣Sdet⁡ΣN,\det K=\det\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((T,S,N')\bigr) =\det\begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_T&\Sigma_{TS}&0\\ \Sigma_{ST}&\Sigma_S&0\\ 0&0&\Sigma_N \end{bmatrix} =\det\Sigma_S\,\det\Sigma_{T\mid S}\,\det\Sigma_N, using in the last step the Schur factorization det⁡Cov⁡((T,S))=det⁡ΣSdet⁡ΣT∣S\det\operatorname{Cov}((T,S))=\det\Sigma_S\,\det\Sigma_{T\mid S}. The same Schur factorization applied to KK in the other block order gives det⁡K=det⁡Mdet⁡Σe\det K=\det M\,\det\Sigma_e, and applied to MM itself gives det⁡M=det⁡ΣS⋅det⁡(Cov⁡(𝐘̂)−Cov⁡(𝐘̂,S)ΣS−1Cov⁡(S,𝐘̂)).\det M=\det\Sigma_S\cdot\det\Bigl(\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y}) -\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf Y},S)\Sigma_S^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(S,\hat{\mathbf Y})\Bigr). It remains to evaluate the conditional block. Remark 10 (Degenerate residuals). If ΣN\Sigma_N is singular, some combination η𝖳𝐘̂\eta^{\mathsf T}\hat{\mathbf Y} equals η𝖳AT\eta^{\mathsf T}AT almost surely. Theorem 11 (Core: the closed form). Corollary 12 (Anchors: the three classical corners). (i) At ρ=0\rho=0, P(g)=(Dg−1)(sg−1)P(g)=(Dg-1)(sg-1) and g⋆=1/Dg^\star=1/D: L(D)=12log⁡2(1/D)L(D)=\tfrac12\log_2(1/D) is the classical rate–distortion function, attained with b=0b=0 by the classical reverse test channel. V. The Rate–Content Region and Misalignment

The work-only endpoint of Theorem 11 does not come for free in rate. This section characterizes the full tradeoff between the two coordinates of (12) for the Gaussian pair source. Throughout, ρ2∈(0,1)\rho^2\in(0,1), τ2>0\tau^2>0, 0<D<10<D<1, and hh, Q0Q_0, Q1Q_1, μc\mu_c are as in the proof of Theorem 11. In the frontier system below, α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] weights rate against conditional content, and γ0=n/(Q0+n)\gamma_0=n/(Q_0+n) and γ1=n/(Q1+n)\gamma_1=n/(Q_1+n) are the two water levels the stationarity system balances: the frontier point at weight α\alpha is (12log⁡2(1/γ0),12log⁡2(1/γ1))\bigl(\tfrac12\log_2(1/\gamma_0),\,\tfrac12\log_2(1/\gamma_1)\bigr).

Theorem 13 (Core: the rate–content region). The closure of the achievable rate–content pairs at distortion DD is the closed convex set whose Pareto frontier is traced by α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] as follows. Let (a,b,n,γ0,γ1)(a,b,n,\gamma_0,\gamma_1), with n>0n>0 and γ0,γ1∈(0,1)\gamma_0,\gamma_1\in(0,1), solve the stationarity system a=1−αγ0−(1−α)γ1,μc=aρs−(1−α)γ1,b=(1−α)γ1μc,(31)\begin{equation*} a=1-\alpha\gamma_0-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1, \qquad \mu_c=\frac{a\rho}{s-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1}, \qquad b=(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\mu_c, \qquad\text{(31)} \end{equation*} n=D−h(a,b),γ0=nQ0+n,γ1=nQ1+n.(32)\begin{equation*} n=D-h(a,b), \qquad \gamma_0=\frac{n}{Q_0+n}, \qquad \gamma_1=\frac{n}{Q_1+n}. \qquad\text{(32)} \end{equation*} The solution exists and is unique at every α\alpha (Proposition 15 below; at α=0\alpha=0 uniqueness also follows from Theorem 11), and the frontier point is (R(α),L(α))=(12log⁡21γ0,12log⁡21γ1),\bigl(R(\alpha),L(\alpha)\bigr) =\Bigl(\tfrac12\log_2\frac1{\gamma_0},\ \tfrac12\log_2\frac1{\gamma_1}\Bigr), achieved by Ŷ=aY+bV+N\widehat{Y}=aY+bV+N, N∼𝒩(0,n)N\sim\mathcal N(0,n). Endpoints: α=1\alpha=1 recovers the classical reverse channel (b=0b=0, a=1−Da=1-D, γ0=D\gamma_0=D, R=12log⁡2(1/D)R=\tfrac12\log_2(1/D)); α=0\alpha=0 recovers the channel and value of Theorem 11 (γ1=1/g⋆\gamma_1=1/g^\star).

Proof. Convexity and scalarization. Both coordinates are convex in the test channel: Lemma 3 and the per-ss decomposition (11) apply verbatim with the sum over ss replaced by an integral against the law of SS, the conditional laws p(t∣s)p(t\mid s) being furnished by disintegration through a regular conditional probability (SS takes values in a standard Borel space). The achievable set of pairs at distortion DD is therefore convex, closed, and upward closed in each coordinate, so every point of its Pareto frontier minimizes one of the weighted objectives Jα:=αI(T;Ŷ)+(1−α)I(T;Ŷ∣S),α∈[0,1],J_\alpha:=\alpha\,I(T;\widehat{Y})+(1-\alpha)\,I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S), \qquad\alpha\in[0,1], over admissible channels, by the supporting-hyperplane argument. At the interior weights each JαJ_\alpha-minimizer is a frontier point; at the endpoint weights α∈{0,1}\alpha\in\{0,1\} this a priori fixes only one coordinate of the minimizer, and the value of the other coordinate is pinned by the uniqueness of the minimizing moments (Proposition 15 below; the argument is run in detail in the proof of Corollary 16 at the end of this section).

The two determinant identities. Fix an admissible channel, centered without loss, with regression coordinates (a,b,n)(a,b,n), n>0n>0, as in the proof of Theorem 11; the Markov moment identity Cov⁡(N′,S)=0\operatorname{Cov}(N',S)=0 holds as there. Lemma 9 applies twice to the same three moments, once with the conditioner SS and once with SS deleted: I(T;Ŷ)≥12log⁡2det⁡ΣTdet⁡Σe0=12log⁡2Q0+nn,I(T;Ŷ∣S)≥12log⁡2det⁡ΣT∣Sdet⁡Σe=12log⁡2Q1+nn,(33)\begin{equation*} I(T;\widehat{Y})\ \ge\ \tfrac12\log_2\frac{\det\Sigma_T}{\det\Sigma_{e0}} =\tfrac12\log_2\frac{Q_0+n}{n}, \qquad I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S)\ \ge\ \tfrac12\log_2\frac{\det\Sigma_{T\mid S}}{\det\Sigma_{e}} =\tfrac12\log_2\frac{Q_1+n}{n}, \qquad\text{(33)} \end{equation*} where Σe0\Sigma_{e0} is the error covariance of the best linear estimate of TT from Ŷ\widehat{Y} alone. The conditional identity is written out in the proof of Theorem 11. The rate identity, in full: with ĉ:=𝔼[TŶ]=ΣT(a,b)𝖳\hat c:=\mathbb{E}[T\widehat{Y}]=\Sigma_T(a,b)^{\mathsf T} and Var⁡Ŷ=Q0+n\operatorname{Var}\widehat{Y}=Q_0+n, Σe0=ΣT−ĉĉ𝖳Q0+n,det⁡Σe0=det⁡ΣT(1−ĉ𝖳ΣT−1ĉQ0+n)=det⁡ΣTnQ0+n,\Sigma_{e0}=\Sigma_T-\frac{\hat c\,\hat c^{\mathsf T}}{Q_0+n}, \qquad \det\Sigma_{e0} =\det\Sigma_T\, \Bigl(1-\frac{\hat c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_T^{-1}\hat c}{Q_0+n}\Bigr) =\det\Sigma_T\,\frac{n}{Q_0+n}, by the rank-one determinant identity det⁡(Σ−ĉĉ𝖳/v)=det⁡Σ(1−ĉ𝖳Σ−1ĉ/v)\det(\Sigma-\hat c\hat c^{\mathsf T}/v) =\det\Sigma\,(1-\hat c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\hat c/v) and ĉ𝖳ΣT−1ĉ=(a,b)ΣT(a,b)𝖳=Q0\hat c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_T^{-1}\hat c =(a,b)\,\Sigma_T\,(a,b)^{\mathsf T}=Q_0.

The weighted moment program. Combining, JαJ_\alpha is bounded below by min(a,b,n)φα(a,b,n):=α2log⁡2Q0+nn+1−α2log⁡2Q1+nns.t.h(a,b)+n≤D,n>0.(34)\begin{equation*} \min_{(a,b,n)}\ \varphi_\alpha(a,b,n):= \frac\alpha2\log_2\frac{Q_0+n}{n} +\frac{1-\alpha}2\log_2\frac{Q_1+n}{n} \quad\text{s.t.}\quad h(a,b)+n\le D,\ n>0 . \qquad\text{(34)} \end{equation*} As in Theorem 11’s proof: φα\varphi_\alpha is strictly decreasing in nn at fixed (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b)\ne(0,0), so the distortion constraint is active at the optimum; on the feasible set Q0≥Q1≥q0>0Q_0\ge Q_1\ge q_0>0, so φα→∞\varphi_\alpha\to\infty as n→0n\to0 and the minimum is attained at an interior stationary point of φα(a,b,D−h(a,b))\varphi_\alpha(a,b,D-h(a,b)).

The gradient identities reduce the first-order system linearly. At a stationary point set γ0=n/(Q0+n)\gamma_0=n/(Q_0+n) and γ1=n/(Q1+n)\gamma_1=n/(Q_1+n), both in (0,1)(0,1). For x∈{a,b}x\in\{a,b\}, using ∂xn=−∂xh\partial_xn=-\partial_xh, α∂x(Q0−h)Q0+n+(1−α)∂x(Q1−h)Q1+n+∂xhn=0;\alpha\,\frac{\partial_x(Q_0-h)}{Q_0+n} +(1-\alpha)\,\frac{\partial_x(Q_1-h)}{Q_1+n} +\frac{\partial_xh}{n}=0 ; multiplying by n/2n/2 and inserting the four gradient identities (25): x=a:αγ0+(1−α)γ1(1−ρμc)+(a+bρ−1)=0,(35)x=b:αγ0ρ+(1−α)γ1(ρ−μc)+(aρ+b−ρ)=0.(36)\begin{align*} x=a:&\quad \alpha\gamma_0+(1-\alpha)\gamma_1(1-\rho\mu_c)+(a+b\rho-1)=0, \qquad\text{(35)}\\ x=b:&\quad \alpha\gamma_0\rho+(1-\alpha)\gamma_1(\rho-\mu_c)+(a\rho+b-\rho)=0 . \qquad\text{(36)} \end{align*} Subtract ρ\rho times (35) from (36): the γ0\gamma_0 terms cancel, the γ1\gamma_1 terms give (1−α)γ1[(ρ−μc)−ρ(1−ρμc)]=−(1−α)γ1μc(1−ρ2)(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\bigl[(\rho-\mu_c)-\rho(1-\rho\mu_c)\bigr] =-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\mu_c(1-\rho^2), and the moment terms give (aρ+b)−ρ(a+bρ)=b(1−ρ2)(a\rho+b)-\rho(a+b\rho)=b(1-\rho^2), so b(1−ρ2)=(1−α)γ1μc(1−ρ2)⇒b=(1−α)γ1μc,b(1-\rho^2)=(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\mu_c(1-\rho^2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\mu_c , dividing by 1−ρ2>01-\rho^2>0, which is in force since ρ2∈(0,1)\rho^2\in(0,1) throughout this section. Equation (35) then reads a+bρ=1−αγ0−(1−α)γ1+(1−α)γ1ρμc=1−αγ0−(1−α)γ1+bρa+b\rho=1-\alpha\gamma_0-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1+(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\rho\mu_c =1-\alpha\gamma_0-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1+b\rho, so a=1−αγ0−(1−α)γ1a=1-\alpha\gamma_0-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1. Finally sμc=aρ+b=aρ+(1−α)γ1μcs\mu_c=a\rho+b=a\rho+(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\mu_c rearranges to μc=aρ/(s−(1−α)γ1)\mu_c=a\rho/\bigl(s-(1-\alpha)\gamma_1\bigr), the denominator being positive since s>1>(1−α)γ1s>1>(1-\alpha)\gamma_1. This is (31); (32) restates the activity of the constraint and the definitions of (γ0,γ1)(\gamma_0,\gamma_1). Conversely, every solution of the system with n>0n>0 is a stationary point of the reduced program, and by Proposition 15 below the program is convex in moment coordinates with a unique minimizer, so the system’s solution is unique and is that minimizer.

Achievability. The jointly Gaussian channel Ŷ=aY+bV+N\widehat{Y}=aY+bV+N, N∼𝒩(0,n)N\sim\mathcal N(0,n), with the optimal (a,b,n)(a,b,n) realizes the same moments and, by the equality clause of Lemma 9, attains both bounds of (33) simultaneously: I(T;Ŷ)=12log⁡2(1/γ0)I(T;\widehat{Y})=\tfrac12\log_2(1/\gamma_0) and I(T;Ŷ∣S)=12log⁡2(1/γ1)I(T;\widehat{Y}\mid S)=\tfrac12\log_2(1/\gamma_1). Hence the value of (34) equals the minimum of JαJ_\alpha, the frontier point is as displayed, and the trace over α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is the entire Pareto boundary.

Endpoints. At α=1\alpha=1, (31) gives b=0b=0 and a=1−γ0a=1-\gamma_0; then h=(1−a)2=γ02h=(1-a)^2=\gamma_0^2, Q0=a2Q_0=a^2, and γ0(Q0+n)=n\gamma_0(Q_0+n)=n forces γ0a2=n(1−γ0)=na\gamma_0a^2=n(1-\gamma_0)=na, so n=γ0an=\gamma_0a; combined with n=D−γ02n=D-\gamma_0^2 this gives γ0(1−γ0)=D−γ02\gamma_0(1-\gamma_0)=D-\gamma_0^2, that is, γ0=D\gamma_0=D, a=1−Da=1-D, n=D(1−D)n=D(1-D): the classical reverse channel. At α=0\alpha=0 the γ0\gamma_0 terms drop from (35)–(36), which become (26) with g=1/γ1g=1/\gamma_1; Theorem 11 identifies γ1=1/g⋆\gamma_1=1/g^\star and the channel (21).

□

Uniqueness at every weight is a convexity statement in moment coordinates. It is cleanest, and no harder, in the whitened frame that Section VII also uses; we set it up once. Since ΣT≻0\Sigma_T\succ0 and 0≺ΣT∣S≼ΣT0\prec\Sigma_{T\mid S}\preceq\Sigma_T, there is a nonsingular WW with WΣTW𝖳=I,WΣT∣SW𝖳=Λ=diag(λ1,…,λp),0≺Λ≼I(37)\begin{equation*} W\Sigma_TW^{\mathsf T}=I, \qquad W\Sigma_{T\mid S}W^{\mathsf T} =\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p), \qquad 0\prec\Lambda\preceq I \qquad\text{(37)} \end{equation*} (factor ΣT=LL𝖳\Sigma_T=LL^{\mathsf T}, diagonalize L−1ΣT∣SL−𝖳=OΛO𝖳L^{-1}\Sigma_{T\mid S}L^{-\mathsf T}=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}, and set W=O𝖳L−1W=O^{\mathsf T}L^{-1}). Write Z=WTZ=WT, so Cov⁡Z=I\operatorname{Cov}Z=I; the described variable becomes Y=y0𝖳ZY=y_0^{\mathsf T}Z with y0=W−𝖳eYy_0=W^{-\mathsf T}e_Y and |y0|2=eY𝖳ΣTeY=1|y_0|^2=e_Y^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_Te_Y=1. A channel with regression vector (a,b)𝖳(a,b)^{\mathsf T} on TT has regression vector c=W−𝖳(a,b)𝖳c=W^{-\mathsf T}(a,b)^{\mathsf T} on ZZ, and Q0=|c|2,Q1=c𝖳Λc,h=|y0−c|2,𝔼(Y−Ŷ)2=|y0−c|2+n.Q_0=|c|^2,\qquad Q_1=c^{\mathsf T}\Lambda c,\qquad h=|y_0-c|^2,\qquad \mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat{Y})^2=|y_0-c|^2+n . Here p=2p=2; Section VII uses p=1+rp=1+r.

Lemma 14 (Matrix convexity of the Schur ratio). Let 𝒵⊆ℝq\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q be convex, a:𝒵→ℝpa:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb{R}^p affine, and σ:𝒵→(0,∞)\sigma:\mathcal Z\to(0,\infty) concave. Then F(z):=a(z)a(z)𝖳σ(z)F(z):=\frac{a(z)\,a(z)^{\mathsf T}}{\sigma(z)} is matrix-convex: F(zt)≼(1−t)F(z0)+tF(z1)F(z_t)\preceq(1-t)F(z_0)+tF(z_1) for all z0,z1∈𝒵z_0,z_1\in\mathcal Z, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], zt=(1−t)z0+tz1z_t=(1-t)z_0+tz_1.

Proof. For σ>0\sigma>0 the Schur-complement criterion states [Waa𝖳σ]≽0⇔W≽aa𝖳σ,\begin{bmatrix}W&a\\ a^{\mathsf T}&\sigma\end{bmatrix}\succeq0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W\succeq\frac{aa^{\mathsf T}}{\sigma}, so F(z)F(z) is the smallest matrix admitted by the criterion at zz. Fix z0,z1,tz_0,z_1,t and abbreviate ai=a(zi)a_i=a(z_i), σi=σ(zi)\sigma_i=\sigma(z_i), Fi=F(zi)F_i=F(z_i). The two positive semidefinite block matrices [F0a0a0𝖳σ0]≽0,[F1a1a1𝖳σ1]≽0\begin{bmatrix}F_0&a_0\\ a_0^{\mathsf T}&\sigma_0\end{bmatrix} \succeq0, \qquad \begin{bmatrix}F_1&a_1\\ a_1^{\mathsf T}&\sigma_1\end{bmatrix} \succeq0 average, with weights (1−t,t)(1-t,t), to [(1−t)F0+tF1a(zt)a(zt)𝖳(1−t)σ0+tσ1]≽0,\begin{bmatrix} (1-t)F_0+tF_1&a(z_t)\\ a(z_t)^{\mathsf T}&(1-t)\sigma_0+t\sigma_1 \end{bmatrix}\succeq0, using affinity of aa in the off-diagonal blocks. Concavity gives σ(zt)≥(1−t)σ0+tσ1\sigma(z_t)\ge(1-t)\sigma_0+t\sigma_1, and adding the positive semidefinite matrix diag(0,σ(zt)−(1−t)σ0−tσ1)\mathrm{diag}\bigl(0,\sigma(z_t)-(1-t)\sigma_0-t\sigma_1\bigr) raises the corner: [(1−t)F0+tF1a(zt)a(zt)𝖳σ(zt)]≽0.\begin{bmatrix} (1-t)F_0+tF_1&a(z_t)\\ a(z_t)^{\mathsf T}&\sigma(z_t) \end{bmatrix}\succeq0 . By the criterion again, (1−t)F0+tF1≽a(zt)a(zt)𝖳/σ(zt)=F(zt)(1-t)F_0+tF_1\succeq a(z_t)a(z_t)^{\mathsf T}/\sigma(z_t)=F(z_t).

□

Proposition 15 (Uniqueness at every weight). In the whitened frame (37), with 0≺Λ≼I0\prec\Lambda\preceq I, |y0|=1|y_0|=1, D∈(0,1)D\in(0,1), and any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], the weighted program (34) (with Q0=|c|2Q_0=|c|^2, Q1=c𝖳ΛcQ_1=c^{\mathsf T}\Lambda c, h=|y0−c|2h=|y_0-c|^2, minimized over (c,n)(c,n)) has a unique minimizer, and every stationary point with n>0n>0 is that minimizer. Since the change of variables c=W−𝖳(a,b)𝖳c=W^{-\mathsf T}(a,b)^{\mathsf T} is a linear bijection, the same holds for the program in the coordinates of Theorem 13.

Proof. Work in the moment coordinates z=(c,v)z=(c,v), v=Var⁡Ŷ=|c|2+nv=\operatorname{Var}\widehat{Y}=|c|^2+n, on the domain 𝒟={(c,v):v>|c|2,1−2y0𝖳c+v≤D},\mathcal D=\bigl\{(c,v):v>|c|^2,\ 1-2y_0^{\mathsf T}c+v\le D\bigr\}, which is convex: v>|c|2v>|c|^2 is the strict epigraph of a convex function, and the distortion constraint h+n=1−2y0𝖳c+v≤Dh+n=1-2y_0^{\mathsf T}c+v\le D is linear in zz. On 𝒟\mathcal D define σ:=v−c𝖳(I−Λ)c=Q1+n>0\sigma:=v-c^{\mathsf T}(I-\Lambda)c=Q_1+n>0 and B0=12log⁡2Q0+nn=−12log⁡2det⁡(I−cc𝖳v),B1=12log⁡2Q1+nn=12log⁡2det⁡Λ−12log⁡2det⁡(Λ−(Λc)(Λc)𝖳σ);\begin{align*} B_0&=\tfrac12\log_2\frac{Q_0+n}{n} =-\tfrac12\log_2\det\Bigl(I-\frac{cc^{\mathsf T}}{v}\Bigr),\\ B_1&=\tfrac12\log_2\frac{Q_1+n}{n} =\tfrac12\log_2\det\Lambda -\tfrac12\log_2\det\Bigl(\Lambda -\frac{(\Lambda c)(\Lambda c)^{\mathsf T}}{\sigma}\Bigr); \end{align*} the first equality holds because det⁡(I−cc𝖳/v)=1−|c|2/v=n/v\det(I-cc^{\mathsf T}/v)=1-|c|^2/v=n/v, the second because det⁡(Λ−(Λc)(Λc)𝖳/σ)=det⁡Λ(1−c𝖳Λc/σ)=det⁡Λ⋅n/σ\det\bigl(\Lambda-(\Lambda c)(\Lambda c)^{\mathsf T}/\sigma\bigr) =\det\Lambda\,\bigl(1-c^{\mathsf T}\Lambda c/\sigma\bigr) =\det\Lambda\cdot n/\sigma.

Convexity. Apply Lemma 14 twice. For B0B_0: z↦cz\mapsto c is affine and z↦vz\mapsto v is affine, hence concave and positive on 𝒟\mathcal D, so W0(z)=cc𝖳/vW_0(z)=cc^{\mathsf T}/v is matrix-convex. Moreover I−W0≻0I-W_0\succ0 on 𝒟\mathcal D, hence invertible: by the Schur criterion, I≻cc𝖳/vI\succ cc^{\mathsf T}/v is equivalent to v−|c|2>0v-|c|^2>0, and v−|c|2=n>0v-|c|^2=n>0 on 𝒟\mathcal D by construction. For B1B_1: z↦Λcz\mapsto\Lambda c is affine and z↦σ=v−c𝖳(I−Λ)c=Q1+nz\mapsto\sigma=v-c^{\mathsf T}(I-\Lambda)c=Q_1+n is concave (affine minus a convex quadratic, I−Λ≽0I-\Lambda\succeq0) and positive on 𝒟\mathcal D (Q1≥0Q_1\ge0, n>0n>0), so W1(z)=(Λc)(Λc)𝖳/σW_1(z)=(\Lambda c)(\Lambda c)^{\mathsf T}/\sigma is matrix-convex, Λ−W1\Lambda-W_1 is matrix-concave, and Λ−W1≻0\Lambda-W_1\succ0 because c𝖳Λc=Q1<Q1+n=σc^{\mathsf T}\Lambda c=Q_1<Q_1+n=\sigma. The map Σ↦−log⁡2det⁡Σ\Sigma\mapsto-\log_2\det\Sigma on positive definite matrices is convex and decreasing in the Löwner order; for the latter, if 0≺A≼B0\prec A\preceq B then B−1/2AB−1/2≼IB^{-1/2}AB^{-1/2}\preceq I has eigenvalues in (0,1](0,1], so det⁡A/det⁡B=det⁡(B−1/2AB−1/2)≤1\det A/\det B=\det(B^{-1/2}AB^{-1/2})\le1, that is, det⁡A≤det⁡B\det A\le\det B. Composing a convex antitone function with a matrix-concave map preserves convexity: for matrix-concave F≻0F\succ0, −log⁡det⁡F(zt)≤−log⁡det⁡((1−t)F(z0)+tF(z1))≤(1−t)(−log⁡det⁡F(z0))+t(−log⁡det⁡F(z1)).-\log\det F(z_t) \;\le\;-\log\det\bigl((1-t)F(z_0)+tF(z_1)\bigr) \;\le\;(1-t)\bigl(-\log\det F(z_0)\bigr) +t\bigl(-\log\det F(z_1)\bigr). Hence B0B_0, B1B_1, and every Bα:=αB0+(1−α)B1B_\alpha:=\alpha B_0+(1-\alpha)B_1 are convex on 𝒟\mathcal D.

Reduction to the active slice. On 𝒟\mathcal D, feasibility forces c≠0c\ne0: from v>|c|2≥0v>|c|^2\ge0 and 1−2y0𝖳c+v≤D1-2y_0^{\mathsf T}c+v\le D, 2y0𝖳c≥1−D+v>1−D>0.(38)\begin{equation*} 2\,y_0^{\mathsf T}c\;\ge\;1-D+v\;>\;1-D\;>\;0 . \qquad\text{(38)} \end{equation*} At fixed c≠0c\ne0 both B0B_0 and B1B_1 strictly decrease in vv (∂v[ln⁡v−ln⁡n]=v−1−n−1<0\partial_v[\ln v-\ln n]=v^{-1}-n^{-1}<0 and ∂v[ln⁡σ−ln⁡n]=σ−1−n−1<0\partial_v[\ln\sigma-\ln n]=\sigma^{-1}-n^{-1}<0, since Q0≥Q1>0Q_0\ge Q_1>0), so every minimizer of BαB_\alpha lies on the active slice v=D−1+2y0𝖳cv=D-1+2y_0^{\mathsf T}c, an affine section of 𝒟\mathcal D. On the slice BαB_\alpha is convex, so its stationary points are exactly its global minimizers and the minimizer set is convex; coercivity as in Theorem 13’s proof gives attainment.

Strictness. Suppose z0≠z1z_0\ne z_1 are both minimizers on the slice, and let ztz_t run over the segment, along which vv and cc are affine in tt. Then BαB_\alpha is affine on the segment, and since B0B_0, B1B_1 are convex and their weighted sum is affine, each BiB_i carrying nonzero weight is affine on the segment. We use twice the following fact: for an affine positive definite matrix segment Σt=(1−t)Σ0+tΣ1\Sigma_t=(1-t)\Sigma_0+t\Sigma_1, the function t↦−log⁡det⁡Σtt\mapsto-\log\det\Sigma_t has second derivative tr⁡[(Σt−1Σ̇)2]≥0\operatorname{tr}\bigl[(\Sigma_t^{-1}\dot\Sigma)^2\bigr]\ge0, which vanishes only if Σ̇=0\dot\Sigma=0, because Σt−1/2Σ̇Σt−1/2\Sigma_t^{-1/2}\dot\Sigma\Sigma_t^{-1/2} is symmetric and a symmetric matrix whose square has zero trace is zero. Moreover, if a matrix-concave FF has −log⁡det⁡F-\log\det F affine on the segment, then squeezing −log⁡det⁡F(zt)≤−log⁡det⁡((1−t)F(z0)+tF(z1))≤-\log\det F(z_t)\le-\log\det\bigl((1-t)F(z_0)+tF(z_1)\bigr)\le the affine interpolant forces both inequalities to be equalities; the second forces F(z0)=F(z1)=:F‾F(z_0)=F(z_1)=:\bar F by the fact just stated, and the first then forces F(zt)≽F‾F(z_t)\succeq\bar F with det⁡F(zt)=det⁡F‾\det F(z_t)=\det\bar F, hence F(zt)=F‾F(z_t)=\bar F for all tt (if A≽B≻0A\succeq B\succ0 and det⁡A=det⁡B\det A=\det B then A=BA=B).

Case α>0\alpha>0, where strictness comes from the forced constancy of the rank-one ratio W0W_0 along the segment: B0B_0 is affine, so W0(zt)=c(t)c(t)𝖳/v(t)W_0(z_t)=c(t)c(t)^{\mathsf T}/v(t) is constant, a rank-one matrix W‾0≠0\bar W_0\ne0 by (38). Then c(t)=θ(t)ec(t)=\theta(t)e for a fixed unit vector ee, with θ\theta affine (a coordinate of the affine cc), and θ(t)2=v(t)(e𝖳W‾0e)\theta(t)^2=v(t)\,(e^{\mathsf T}\bar W_0e) with vv affine. An affine function whose square is affine is constant, so θ\theta, hence cc, hence v=D−1+2y0𝖳cv=D-1+2y_0^{\mathsf T}c, is constant: z0=z1z_0=z_1, a contradiction.

Corollary 18 (Consequence: LL is not determined by the reduced marginal (Y,S)(Y,S)).

Two instances whose (Y,S)(Y,S) joint laws are equivalent up to bijective scaling can have different minimal conditional content: the instances (ρ2,τ2)=(12,0)(\rho^2,\tau^2)=(\tfrac12,0) and (34,12)(\tfrac34,\tfrac12) have ρYS2=12\rho_{YS}^2=\tfrac12 in both cases, yet L=1.1610L=1.1610 versus 1.21051.2105 bits at D=0.1D=0.1, and L=0.3685L=0.3685 versus 0.52280.5228 bits at D=0.3D=0.3, in both cases strictly below the value of Steinberg’s scalar formula on the reduced pair (1.22971.2297 and 0.55770.5577 bits respectively). So no functional of the (Y,S)(Y,S) joint law, in particular neither Steinberg’s scalar formula evaluated on (Y,S)(Y,S) nor Gray’s, can equal LL. This is no departure from Steinberg’s functional, whose source here is the full pair (Y,V)(Y,V); it shows the augmentation is load-bearing: the encoder’s access to the clean context VV enters the function.

The two instances share the (Y,S)(Y,S) joint law: in both, YY is standard and ρYS2=Cov⁡(Y,S)2/Var⁡S=ρ2/s\rho_{YS}^2=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,S)^2/\operatorname{Var}S=\rho^2/s equals 12\tfrac12, namely (12)/1(\tfrac12)/1 and (34)/(32)(\tfrac34)/(\tfrac32), and rescaling SS changes none of the quantities considered: a bijective scaling S↦κSS\mapsto\kappa S, κ≠0\kappa\ne0, leaves the generated σ\sigma-algebra unchanged, σ(κS)=σ(S)\sigma(\kappa S)=\sigma(S), so every conditional mutual information given SS, and with it L(D)L(D), is invariant, and the two instances may be normalized to a common (Y,S)(Y,S) law.

First instance, (ρ2,τ2)=(12,0)(\rho^2,\tau^2)=(\tfrac12,0): the context is clean. This instance sits at the boundary τ2=0\tau^2=0 excluded by the standing assumption τ2>0\tau^2>0 of Section III, so its value is supplied not by Theorem 11 but directly by Proposition 8(ii), which is proved at τ2=0\tau^2=0 (and which the τ2→0\tau^2\to0 anchor of Corollary 12 matches in the limit). The value of Steinberg’s scalar formula on the reduced pair: an encoder observing YY alone pays the marginalized-class optimum of Section IV, the scalar-corner value 12log⁡2[(1−ρYS2+ρYS2D)/D]\tfrac12\log_2\bigl[(1-\rho_{YS}^2+\rho_{YS}^2D)/D\bigr] at ρYS2=12\rho_{YS}^2=\tfrac12, that is, 12log⁡2[(1+D)/(2D)]\tfrac12\log_2\bigl[(1+D)/(2D)\bigr]: 12log⁡25.5=1.2297\tfrac12\log_2 5.5=1.2297 bits at D=0.1D=0.1, and 12log⁡2(13/6)=0.5577\tfrac12\log_2(13/6)=0.5577 bits at D=0.3D=0.3.
